newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Instability could wreck Belgium's EMU hopes - minister.
newsitem.headline: Instability could wreck Belgium's EMU hopes - minister.

text.p: Belgium's government must stay in power or the scandal-torn country would suffer fresh political and financial market doubts about its likely entry into Europe's currency union, a government minister said.
"Relinquishing the reins now would have disastrous consequences," Budget Minister Herman van Rompuy told the daily De Financieel-Economische Tijd in an interview published on Friday.

The ruling coalition has been in the eye of various storms since last August, although only the latest scandal over corruption in one of the four coalition parties -- that of French-speaking PS socialists -- has come close to toppling the government.
Three PS officials have been in jail for weeks and a ranking party member lost his parliamentary immunity on Thursday over charges of receiving stolen goods, fraud and money laundering.

An ex-PS chairman, who held high office in the regional government of Wallonia, Belgium's francophone southern half, and was chairman of a body controlling a major bank, resigned those posts on Thursday over his alleged involvement in the scandal.

The allegations, centring on 45 million Belgian francs ($1.3 million) paid to the PS by French defense firm Dassault to win a large order in the late 1980s, have raised serious doubts over the credibility of the PS and its suitability to govern.
Dassault, whose chief Serge Dassault is the subject of an international arrest warrant issued by Belgium, has denied any wrongdoing.
Fingers of blame have increasingly pointed at current PS chairman Philippe Busquin who like his predecessor Guy Spitaels denies all knowledge of the money or the accounts.
Busquin faces re-election to the PS chair this weekend.
Budget Minister Van Rompuy said it would be a disservice to Belgium to change coalition partners now or hold elections, as opposition parties are demanding.
"The question is whether political instability, let alone new elections, is in Belgium's interest," he said.

The centre-left government of Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene needs the PS, and the unions which come under its influence, on its side to continue its programmes of social security system and budget reforms and job creation.
It still faces a round of delicate manoeuvring to reform public sector pensions -- one of many of the achievements Belgians feel strongly about and willing to strike over.
The reforms are needed to make the Belgian economy fit to join the European Union's single currency, the euro.

Any interruption to the goverment's drive to cut debt and deficits might be seen as an open invitation to currency speculators to attack the franc and thus ruin Belgium's chances of being in the vanguard of those joining the euro.
The franc has already been under pressure because of the woes over the PS, but Dehaene's single-minded single currency ambition has ridden rough shod over this and other crises.
